name: Fond du Lac agreement under the Nelson Act, signed November 21, 1889
aka: Nelson Act cession, Fond du Lac band
Act for the relief and civilization of the Chippewa Indians in the State of Minnesota (Nelson Act)
citation: Act of January 14, 1889, ch. 24, 25 Stat. 642; agreement printed in H. R. Ex. Doc. 247, 51st Cong., 1st sess.
nations: Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa
promises: Section 1: an Indian already holding an allotment on the reservation not to be deprived of it or disturbed except by his own separate consent; the cession valid only if assented to in writing by two-thirds of the band's male adults.
Section 3: allotments in severalty; any Indian could take his allotment on the reservation where he lived instead of removing to White Earth.
Sections 4 and 5: pine lands examined, appraised at no less than $3 per thousand feet of timber, and sold at public auction in 40-acre lots for no less than the appraised value.
Section 6: other ceded land sold only to actual settlers under the homestead law at $1.25 an acre.

Section 7: all net proceeds held in the Treasury as a permanent fund for all the Chippewa in Minnesota at 5% interest, paid yearly for fifty years, with a quarter of the interest for schools, and the fund then divided among them in equal shares.

breaches.what: The Minnesota Chippewa Tribe, of which the Fond du Lac Band is a member, claimed in Indian Claims Commission Dockets 19 and 188 that Nelson Act land and timber proceeds were misspent and that land and timber were sold for less than full value. The claims were settled for $20 million, which the Court of Federal Claims awarded in May 1999.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Minnesota Chippewa Tribe v. United States, Dockets 19 and 188 (settlement), as described in the Bureau of Indian Affairs' testimony to the House Subcommittee on Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, March 1, 2012

source.title: Testimony of Mike Black, Director, Bureau of Indian Affairs, on H.R. 1272, Minnesota Chippewa Tribe Judgment Fund Distribution Act (March 1, 2012)

landTaken: Royce records that the band ceded to the United States all its title and interest in the Fond du Lac reservation (Royce area 338, set apart by the 1854 treaty with a promise of at least 100,000 acres), and its rights in the part of the Red Lake reservation not needed for allotments. Under the Act, land not allotted was to be sold for the Chippewa fund.
compensation: The net proceeds of sales were to go into the Chippewa permanent fund (Section 7). The Bureau of Indian Affairs testified in 2012 that after the fifty years there were no remaining funds to distribute in equal shares. The 1999 settlement of $20 million covers all six member bands of the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe.
today: Royce records an earlier attempt on this reserve under the Act of May 29, 1872: it was appraised and offered for sale on the representation that the Indians had consented, but with few exceptions they refused to remove, declaring that their alleged assent was fraudulent, and removal failed. In 2012 the Bureau of Indian Affairs supported a bill to distribute the 1999 settlement funds; whether it became law was not checked.

plain.promised: Allotments where people lived, no one's allotment taken without consent, and all land and timber sale money held in a fund for all Minnesota Chippewa at 5% interest for fifty years, then shared equally.
plain.happened: The Minnesota Chippewa Tribe, which includes the Fond du Lac Band, claimed the sale money was misspent and land and timber sold below full value. No formal finding specific to this cession has been located.
plain.today: The claims were settled for $20 million in 1999, covering all six member bands. The Bureau of Indian Affairs said in 2012 no fund was left to share out. Whether the settlement money was distributed was not checked.

nationVoice.summary: No Fond du Lac Band statement was found; Leech Lake, a fellow member band of the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe, told the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs in 2012 through Chairman Arthur LaRose that the Nelson Act opened the bands' treaty-protected reservations to settlers and timber companies in clear violation of existing treaties, and that the Tribe's own appraisal for the $20 million settlement put Fond du Lac's share of the land and timber damages at 10.2 percent.

openQuestions: treaties.json error: presentDayTribes for this entry lists eight bands but not the Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa, the band that signed it. The scheduleTribes name 'Chippewa of the Mississippi and Lake Superior' is generic; Royce's schedule names the Fond du Lac Chippewa.
The 1999 settlement is a compromise and is recorded as litigation, not a finding. No court or Commission finding specific to the Fond du Lac cession was found.

Royce's account of the 1872 attempt (the band calling its alleged assent fraudulent) is a government publication's description, not a finding, and concerns the 1872 Act rather than this agreement; the Act of May 29, 1872 was not opened.
The agreement itself (H. R. Ex. Doc. 247, 51st Cong., 1st sess.) was not opened; the date and terms are from Royce and the Act.

How much of the reservation passed out of Indian hands after allotment was not taken from a primary source. The Fond du Lac Band's own account was not found in this pass; Senate testimony by a Minnesota Chippewa Tribe leader could not be downloaded.
